units.text: Start with the upper-left panel. Measure round-trip latency and acceptable variation before choosing connectivity. Then compare those requirements with where the application will run.
Move to capacity and growth on the right. Size normal demand, bursts and migration traffic. A backup path must carry the critical workload, not merely establish a connection.

Compare the middle panels. Private transport and encryption are separate requirements. Resilience also depends on independent devices, circuits, providers and locations; two links can still share one failure.
Return to the full slide. Document acceptable interruption, operational effort and cost. Select the design against those requirements, then test whether the workload still meets them during failure.

Look at the VPN panel on the left. IPsec protects traffic between tunnel endpoints. Internet-based VPN can be established without a dedicated circuit, but performance depends on the underlying path and tunnel configuration.

Move to Direct Connect on the right. It provides a dedicated network connection into AWS. Plan delivery, capacity and physical diversity; private connectivity does not mean traffic is encrypted by default.

Follow the lower row. Combine Direct Connect with VPN backup, or use an IPsec overlay when appropriate. Size the fallback for critical demand and examine equipment, route policy and shared dependencies.
With the complete slide visible, keep three decisions separate: private connectivity, encryption and resilience. A design that satisfies one requirement does not automatically satisfy the other two.

Begin on the left. Each Site-to-Site VPN connection includes two tunnels terminating in different Availability Zones. Configure both so maintenance or an AWS-side tunnel failure has an alternative path.

Inspect the customer-side panel. Two tunnels terminating on one customer router still depend on that device. Additional connections and independent equipment help, but shared circuits, power or locations can remain failure points.

Read the lower row from left to right. Verify route failover and the return path, test application recovery, then exercise tunnel, device and circuit failures. Restored routing does not guarantee that existing sessions survive.

Review the full original slide. Count independent failure domains rather than tunnels alone. Measure recovery against the workload target, including the time the application needs after the network path changes.
Start in the left panel. A virtual private gateway attaches to one VPC and provides managed Site-to-Site VPN termination. This option does not support VPN equal-cost multipath routing.

Move to the Transit Gateway panel. The regional hub connects VPCs and on-premises networks. VPN equal-cost multipath requires dynamic routing and compatible advertised routes; the gateway configuration must also enable the feature.

Inspect the lower row. Configure routes in both directions, use transit route tables to control reachability, and retain security controls. Gateway choice does not remove the need to examine tunnels and customer-side dependencies.

Return to the unchanged full slide. Choose the gateway for the required connectivity scope, then validate routing, access and failover independently. A shared hub is a topology choice, not proof of resilience.
